newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Mideast diplomacy intensifies after suicide attack.
newsitem.headline: Mideast diplomacy intensifies after suicide attack.

text.p: Middle Eastern leaders are crisscrossing the region in search of a way out of the acute crisis in Israeli-PLO peacemaking, deepened by last week's suicide bombings in a Jerusalem street market.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat was in Amman for late-night talks with Jordan's King Hussein. Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy is due to meet Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak in Cairo on Tuesday.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will host King Hussein on Wednesday, Netanyahu's office said on Monday.
The meetings are a prelude to a visit to the region by U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross expected later this week.
The intense diplomacy comes as Palestinians have begun to feel the bite of an Israeli clampdown imposed after two Arab bombers killed 13 people and wounded 170 on Wednesday.
Only after the Palestinian Authority begins to crush Islamic militants, says Netanyahu, will Israel ease its restrictions.

"The Palestinian Authority must decide what type of regime it is, a regime that fights terrorism like Jordan and Egypt, or a regime that encourages terrorism like Iraq and Iran," he told reporters on Monday.
"If it decides to continue as a regime that does not fight terrorism...we will continue our measures," he said.

After the bombing, Netanyahu called a halt to peace talks with the PLO and sealed off the West Bank and Gaza, disrupting Palestinian trade and barring tens of thousands of Arab workers from reaching their workplaces in the Jewish state.
Israel has rounded up scores of suspected militants and threatened to reenter PLO-ruled areas unless Arafat clamps down in territory he controls.
The Palestinian Health Ministry said on Monday that Israel's sealing off of the West Bank and Gaza was causing widespread medical problems.

It said Palestinian medical personnel and supplies were unable to reach hospitals, pregnant village women were unable to reach city hospitals and that patients requiring urgent treatment in Israel or other countries were in danger.

The Agriculture Ministry said Palestinian farmers were unable to move produce out of their home districts, leaving fruit and vegetables to rot. The Industry Ministry said West Bank and Gaza factories were losing $1.8 million per day.
Palestinians have said the Israeli measures are collective punishments that weaken Arafat and strengthen extremist forces.

Europe's Middle East peace envoy Miguel Angel Moratinos concurred. "We cannot really understand some measures that instead of bringing security are bringing insecurity," he said after meeting Arafat on Monday.
Moratinos failed to persuade Netanyahu to lift the siege.

"The prime minister told Moratinos that Israel was acting against terror and not against the Palestinian people...and that Israel was taking different steps in order to pressure the Palestinian Authority to fulfil its obligations," Netanyahu's office said in a statement on Monday.

Israel's Treasury said on Monday it had frozen the transfer of $70 million in VAT and customs duties it owes the Palestinian Authority under a 1994 economic protocol, until the Authority steps up its war against anti-Israel violence.
The move will deepen the Palestinian Authority's financial crisis and make it difficult to cover operating costs and pay public sector salaries.
Israel transferred some 1.2 billion shekels ($339 million) to the Palestinian Authority in 1996. The Authority's official 1997 budget stands at $866 million.

Palestinians suspended security cooperation with Israel after Netanyahu allowed the beginning of the construction of a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in March, but say they have nonetheless worked to foil attacks by militants opposed to the peace process since then.
Political sources in Jerusalem said senior PLO official Mahmoud Abbas telephoned Levy on Arafat's behalf to promise a tougher PLO stand on attacks like the suicide bombings.
Levy said on Monday that Israel did not want the collapse of the Authority but that it had to fight militants.

The perpetrators of the latest suicide attacks remain unknown. A leaflet issued in the name of the Islamist Hamas group claimed responsibility but Israeli and PLO officials have questioned its authenticity.
